_comment: FACTORtv — THE ARCHIVE BROADCAST, and the grid.
Pre-2000 racing is presented as a fixture from the archive: Brett
Calloway leads, Chuck Brannigan alongside. Both are MODERN broadcasters
watching old footage and calling it live.
THE RULES THESE ARE WRITTEN TO — all of them easy to break, and all of
them break immersion loudly when broken:
1. NEITHER OF THEM WAS THERE. No 'I remember this one', no 'I raced
against these men'. Brett is a WEC champion and Chuck a NASCAR Cup
champion; neither has ever driven a Formula One car, and neither was
in the race being shown.
2. THEY DO NOT KNOW HOW IT ENDS. The user is driving it. 'Of course, we
all know what happened next' is false and ruins a career season.
3. NO YEARS, NO CIRCUIT HISTORY, NO REAL RESULTS. The cars and tracks in
any session are an approximation of a PERIOD assembled from whatever
mods exist, not a reconstruction of a specific event. Say 'this era',
never 'the 1988 season'.
4. CAR AND ERA CHARACTER ONLY. What these machines demanded of a driver
is always true and always safe. What happened at a named race is
neither.
Gated by year in the pool entries and by the play-by-play SEAT in
cast.py — before 2000 Brett is in the chair, and these lines come with
him. `archive_*` categories are offered only on historic sessions.
Slots: {trk} circuit, {cls} car class, {series} field, {grid} where the
subject started, {n} a count, {pos} their place now.

archive_open.t: Welcome along to a fixture from the archive. Brett Calloway with you, Chuck Brannigan alongside me.
We're going back for this one — an archive fixture, called as it happened.
A race from the vault today, and Chuck's here to make sense of it with me.
This is one from the archive, and it's a proper reminder of what these machines were.
Out of the archive and onto your screen. Let's watch it unfold.
An old fixture, restored and running again. Brett Calloway with you.

archive_era.t: No traction control, no launch control, no help of any kind. Everything you see is the driver.
These are manual gearboxes. A missed shift here costs an engine, not a tenth.
Look at how much they're moving in the cockpit. There's no power steering to hide behind.
Skinny tyres, enormous power, and a driver holding the two together. That's the whole era.
Cars of this period punished you immediately. There was no margin built in anywhere.
Nobody in that field has a screen telling them what the car is doing. It's all through the seat.
Brakes of this era faded. You planned a race around them, not just a lap.
That's a lot of horsepower and very little downforce. It moves under them constantly.
Safety was an afterthought in this period, and every driver out there knows it.
Racing like this asked a different question of a driver. Not 'how fast', but 'how long can you keep this up'.

archive_watch.t: Worth remembering how little these drivers had to help them.
You don't see driving like this any more.
This is why footage of this era is still worth watching.
Every one of these laps was hand-made. Nothing about it is automatic.
A different sport, in a lot of ways. Same instinct, though.
I never raced anything like that, and watching it I'm quietly relieved.
In a stock car you had weight and time. These men have neither.
This is the sort of thing that doesn't survive into the modern game.
Machines like this asked for a kind of bravery the sport has since engineered out.
